candidate.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — safe disposal of hazardous/contaminated materials
candidate.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — healthcare waste segregation
candidate.educational_objective: Differentiate sharps, blood-contaminated regulated waste, and pharmaceutical waste disposal streams in healthcare settings.

options.A: Use the applicable separate waste streams: a sharps container for the contaminated sharp, regulated-waste handling for the blood-saturated dressing, and pharmaceutical-waste procedures for the unused medication
options.B: Place all three items in ordinary trash because special disposal applies only to laboratory waste
options.C: Use a sharps container for the needle but place the blood-saturated dressing and unused medication in ordinary trash without further assessment
options.D: Place all three items in one biohazard bag because pharmaceutical waste follows the same rules as every blood-contaminated item

candidate.rationale: OSHA defines contaminated sharps and items that would release blood or other potentially infectious material if compressed as regulated waste requiring appropriate containment and disposal. EPA separately requires healthcare facilities to manage pharmaceutical waste under applicable federal, state, and local rules, including RCRA requirements when the pharmaceutical is hazardous waste. A correctly separates these waste categories instead of assuming one universal container. A is correct.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Contaminated sharps and blood-saturated materials meeting OSHA's regulated-waste definition require regulated handling; healthcare-generated pharmaceutical waste is managed under applicable pharmaceutical/hazardous-waste rules rather than a generic clinical-waste stream.
candidate.source_document_title: 29 CFR 1910.1030 Bloodborne Pathogens; Information for Hospitals, Pharmacies and Other Businesses that Have Medicines to Dispose
candidate.source_locator: OSHA 1910.1030(d)(4)(iii) regulated waste and contaminated sharps; EPA Healthcare Facilities Must Comply with RCRA section
candidate.source_organization: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA); U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
candidate.source_version_date: OSHA standard current; EPA page current in 2026, accessed 2026-08-17
candidate.stem: After care, a nurse must discard a contaminated sharp, a dressing saturated enough to release blood if compressed, and unused medication. Which principle is correct?
